Bill Cowden, PAA#1 and George Sellett met us at the airport and escorted us
to the Intercontinental Mandarin, a 600 room 20 story hotel on Victoria
Post Office just behind the ferry landing.
Our room looks out on the harbor with its constantly changing seene of
ferry boats, there are & crossing as I write this line, hundreds of junks
freighters, from all over the world with a few war ships and a passenger
liner or two. Most of the freighters never touch shore, they are unloaded
and loaded by a swarn of small craft coming along side and leaving all day
and all night.
Wed. Dec. 9th•
We tended to tickets changing money etc. in the morning.
George Sellett came by for us about one o'clock and we drove to his house for
lunch.
We crossed to the mainland by auto ferry and then out Nathan road
by the old Peninsula Hotel and between apartment buildings, mostly new, to
the mountains that mark the beginning of the "leased territory". We climbed
up and up along a perfect road to the Carleton Hotel and just beyond that is
George's new "estate". We drove through a gate to find ourselves in a small
garden full of those wonderful chrysanthemums such as only Chinese gardeners
can grow.
The ground floor of the stone house is taken up with a screen
which partly hides a rumpus room which the former owner had for the .
children. A winding stairway leads to an upper floor with bedrooms, 3, each
with bath to the right and to the left a larger living room with roam high
sliğing glass doors which open on a wide terrace which overlooks the whold
of Hong Kong. From the terrace the land falls away steeply to another
terrace and then another 20 feet down to a second with a small swimming
pool and then yet another terrace which is his truck garden. It is a real
gem. The gouse is full of beautiful Chinese furniture. George has a chauffeur
cook, gardener, coolie
and wash anah, quite an establishment and not the
least of the attractions.
We did not get home until late so had an early
snack (after George's enormous steak lunch) and to bed early. My cold is
better.
Thurs. Dec. 10t4h Shopping. One interesting government development in
Kowloon was the reclaiming of a large tract of tidal shallowa where a complex
of apartments surrounds a harbor and provides a perfect shelter for junks
and small boats during typhoons or rough weather.
We have fairly definite plans (for us) now.
We leave here at 1 p.n. on
Dec. 16 for Manila and leave there on the 20th for Honolulu arriving the
same day (thanks to gaining a day crossing the International Date line).
You will no doubt wonder about the Chinese Communists, and so do we.
Outwardly they and China might as well be five thousand miles away. The
bee hive which is Hong Kong goes on as though everyone expected to be here
forever.
The government has just finished a 1,000 bed hospital, a
mountain is being truncated to provide space for another apartment, thousands
of men work around the clock on new buildings, in factories and on docks.
The first time I was here after the Communist take-over in China the
Communist flag was everywhere.
The next time about five years later I saw
a few and this time none.
Real Estate prices in the heart of Kowloon or
Victoria (Hongkong) are higher than New York, something like 500 U.s. dollars
per square foot.
Friday Dec. 11
We had a trip by car all around this island with coffee
at the Repulse Bay Hotel where we lived for a while.
Then we had lunch
at the Peiving restaurant with C.H. (Patty Woo. Others there were Mr. and
Mrs. Bill Cowden, PAA#1, George Sellett and my old friend Nixon, former
Postal Commissioner at Canton.
We had all of our old favorites, Pekin
duck, sharks fin soup, mandarin fish, chicken and walnuts, bahboo shoots,
